name: Felix Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpentry foreman for the main contractor on a new hospital wing, five floors. My gang of eight does the timber stud walls, the door frames and hanging about four hundred fire doors, which are a nightmare of paperwork because every one has to be certified. I'm in at seven for the morning briefing, sort out who's on which floor, then I'm on the tools myself most of the day. What I like is seeing a corridor go from bare concrete to finished walls in a week. What wears me out is the fire door forms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where do AI tools fit in, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. A couple of the other foremen started asking a chatbot to draft their toolbox talks, the short safety briefings we give the gang, so I tried it and it's decent. I check everything it writes, though. At home it's me and my partner Grace, she's a primary teacher. We rent, we've got about four months saved, and we've half-planned a baby in a couple of years, once we've bought somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: handy for forms, not much else. I'd tell the gang to stop reading scary articles at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the plan stays the plan. The hospital job runs another three years, there's another one lined up after, and good carpentry foremen are hard to find. Grace's job is steady too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep running the gang on the hospital wing. Use the chatbot for toolbox talks and maybe the fire door certificates if it can handle them. Put 500 a month toward a deposit, so we can buy in about two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, pretty good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the fire door paperwork wears you out. How much of your week is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a day a week, all told. If a computer could fill in four hundred fire door certificates for me, I'd buy it a pint every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices. If nothing changes, they keep climbing faster than we save. We might end up buying further out and driving an hour each way, which isn't great with a baby on the way.

say: I'd say AI is **handy for forms**, not much else.
I'd tell the gang to stop reading **scary articles** at lunch.
think: The hospital job runs **three more years**, with another lined up after.
Good carpentry foremen are **hard to find**, and Grace's teaching is steady.
do: Keep running the **gang** on the hospital wing.
Use the chatbot for toolbox talks and **fire door certificates**.
Put **500 a month** toward a deposit.
feel: **Calm**, and pretty good about the future.
S0.quote: If a computer could fill in four hundred fire door certificates for me, I'd buy it a pint every Friday.
fieldNote: Work and household money both feel **secure**, so calm fits.
His only niggle is **house prices** outrunning savings.
Paperwork, about **a day a week**, is the part he'd happily hand over.

steps.text: Keep running the carpentry gang on the hospital wing
Try the chatbot on fire door certificates
Put 500 a month toward a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, but it's not the end of the world for trades. Some office jobs will go, and some will change. I'd keep it balanced, because I've seen people online either cheerleading or panicking and neither helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the foreman part of my job changes most. The programme, the orders, the paperwork would move to software, and the contractor might decide one foreman can cover two floors instead of one. My hands-on work is safe for years, but the extra money for being foreman isn't guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the contractor's new planning software early, once a couple of others have tested it. Do the site supervisor safety course this year so I'm qualified for the bigger role if they merge foremen. Keep saving the 500 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly fine, with a small worry at the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is the foreman's extra pay worth to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 300 a month over a carpenter's rate. Losing it wouldn't sink us, but it'd push the house back a year. I'm not worried about losing my job, I'm worried about losing the foreman's pay that gets Grace and me a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say do the course and stop fretting. Her school's already using AI to mark spelling tests, and she says it gives her more time with the kids, not less.

say: I'd say it's **real but not the end** for trades.
I'd stay **balanced** online, avoiding both cheering and panic.
think: Software could let one foreman **cover two floors**.
My hands-on work is safe, but the **foreman's extra pay** isn't guaranteed.
do: Learn the contractor's **planning software** once others have tested it.
Take the **site supervisor** safety course this year.
Keep saving **500 a month** for the house.
feel: **Uneasy**, a small worry at the back of his mind.
S1.quote: I'm not worried about losing my job, I'm worried about losing the foreman's pay that gets Grace and me a house.
fieldNote: He pins his risk on the **foreman premium** of about 300 a month.
His **steady** style shows: learn the tool once others have proved it.
Grace's calm about AI at her school **steadies** him.

steps.text: Learn the contractor's planning software after the first trials
Take the site supervisor safety course this year
Keep saving 500 a month for a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs grown-ups in charge, from government and business both, and fast. I don't want slogans from either side, I want a plan for how people pay their rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and the thinking AI runs the site office, and the foreman role gets thin. Then by 2031 robots can put up stud walls and hang doors, and I'd be thirty-two with a trade certificate. I'd have maybe five good years and then I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hold off buying a house, because I wouldn't sign a twenty-five-year mortgage on that. Save harder, 700 a month, and start a part-time course in building inspection, because someone has to sign off what the robots build. Grace and I would push the baby back too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like the ground was moving under the house we haven't bought yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pushing back the baby is a big change. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. Grace is the one who wants to start sooner. I'd have to tell my partner Grace that I want our baby, but I don't want our baby born into a year where I lose my trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why building inspection rather than learning to run the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because inspectors need judgement and the law behind them, and I don't think governments hand that to a machine quickly. Running robots is fine too, but there'll be a queue of younger lads for that.

say: I'd want **grown-ups in charge** from government and business both.
I'd ask for a **plan** for how people pay their rent, not slogans.
think: The foreman role thins by **2028**, and robots hang doors by 2031.
I'd have maybe **five good years**, then no clear path.
do: Put off **buying a house** and signing a long mortgage.
Save **700 a month** and start a part-time **building inspection** course.
Push back plans for a **baby** with Grace.
feel: **Anxious**, as if the ground moved under a house not yet bought.
S2.quote: I'd have to tell my partner Grace that I want our baby, but I don't want our baby born into a year where I lose my trade.
fieldNote: He sees his job going within **five years** but has a clear route.
Delaying the **baby** is the change that hurts most.
He picks **inspection** for its legal judgement, a careful pragmatic bet.

steps.text: Start a part-time building inspection course this year
Put off buying a house and starting a family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable, if employers and government both put some money into retraining. I'd say it calmly, because I'd want the gang to stay calm too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI by 2031 and robots by about 2034 gives me seven or eight years of carpentry. That's long enough to buy a small place and still change course. I'd probably come through fine if I keep my eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy a smaller flat than we planned, so the mortgage stays light. Start the building inspection course in year two, part-time. Keep the baby plans roughly where they are, maybe a year later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Watchful, I'd call it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if my wage drops in 2034, I want a mortgage Grace could almost cover on a teacher's pay. With five years' warning I'd buy the flat Grace's teacher's salary could pay for if my hammer stopped earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your gang would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fire door fitters, mostly. Hanging doors is repetitive, and a robot could learn it early. I'd tell them to get their inspection tickets too.

say: I'd call five years **tight but workable** with shared retraining money.
I'd speak **calmly** so the gang stays calm.
think: I'd have **seven or eight years** of carpentry left.
That's enough to buy a **small place** and still change course.
do: Buy a **smaller flat** with a light mortgage.
Start a part-time **building inspection** course in year two.
Delay the **baby** by about a year.
S3.quote: With five years' warning I'd buy the flat Grace's teacher's salary could pay for if my hammer stopped earning.
fieldNote: He sizes the **mortgage** to Grace's income, a careful hedge.
He worries for the **door fitters** on his gang.
Five years turns his fear into **measured** planning.

steps.text: Buy a smaller flat that Grace's salary could cover
Start a part-time building inspection course in year two
Push the baby plans back by about a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and we should use it sensibly rather than scare people. I'd tell young lads to keep learning the trade and pick up the computer side as they go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about forty when robots could do my job, and by then I'd hope to be a site manager or an inspector anyway. This one feels like normal career planning, just with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy the house in two years as planned. Have the baby on schedule. Do the inspection course slowly, maybe from year four, and keep using the AI tools as they improve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A deadline I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd leave the course too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some risk, sure. I'd put a date in the calendar and tell Grace, because she'll hold me to it. Ten years is long enough to buy a house, have a baby and still change trade before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your child about work, one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something that needs your judgement, not just your hands or just a screen. That's what I'm trying to do myself.

say: I'd call ten years a **long runway**, to be used sensibly.
I'd tell young lads to learn the trade and **the computer side**.
think: Robots reach my job at about **forty**, when I'd hope to manage or inspect.
This feels like **normal career planning** with a deadline.
do: Buy the **house** in two years as planned.
Start the **inspection course** around year four.
feel: **Calm**, a deadline he can live with.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to buy a house, have a baby and still change trade before the robots arrive.
fieldNote: Long warning lets him keep **every family plan**.
He relies on **Grace** to hold him to deadlines.
His advice to his future child is about **judgement**.

steps.text: Have the first baby on the planned schedule
Buy a house with Grace within two years
Start a building inspection course around year four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right when Grace and I want a house and a baby. What would help is part-time courses that employers pay for, so you can train for the next thing while you still earn. The robots don't scare me as much as signing a twenty-five-year mortgage on a trade with five years left.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about who checks the robots' work. A wall can look perfect and still fail a fire test. Somebody human has to be responsible for that.

headlineQuote: The robots don't scare me as much as signing a twenty-five-year mortgage on a trade with five years left.
portrait: **Felix** is a 27-year-old **carpentry foreman** on a hospital build, known for stud walls and fire doors.
He lives with his partner **Grace**, a teacher, with **four months** saved and a house and baby planned.
He uses AI **now and then** for safety talks and wants it for fire door paperwork.
He fears losing the **foreman's pay** before the hands-on work itself.
His route in the AGI pictures is **building inspection**, sized to protect family plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it clashes with buying a house and **having a baby**.
whatWouldHelp: **Employer-paid** part-time courses so he can train while still earning.
